To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
PHD inhibition with FG‐4095 stimulates angiogenesis and alveolar development and improves pulmonary function in a preterm baboon model of BPD.
inhibition of proly hydroxylase‐containing proteins in a primate model of BPD improves lung function, increases alveolar surface, increases surfactant protein B, and increases alveolarization.
activation of HIF by inhibition of PHDs improves the growth and function of the lungs in a primate model of BPD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying the pathogenesis and pathophysiology of bronchopulmonary dyspnea (BPD) in preterm infants.
the role of hypoxia-inducible factors (and the oxygen sensors that regulate them) in the pathophysiology of lung disease in premature infants.
the role of the transcription factor hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) in the development of lung disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of PHD inhibitors in preterm baboons with chronic lung disease of the newborn is a novel and effective treatment that may be useful in the treatment of human BPD.
